subject: swimming pool
title: What If You Went Swimming Right After Eating?

scenes.text: What if you jumped in the pool right after lunch? The thirty-minute rule has a surprising origin.
A 1908 scouting handbook told boys to wait ninety minutes, or risk deadly cramps.
Your stomach does pull extra blood to digest, but nowhere near enough to stop your arms and legs.
In a 1968 study, swimmers ate a heavy breakfast and swam. Not one got cramps.
The Red Cross reviewed the evidence and found eating doesn't raise drowning risk. The worst you'll get is a side stitch.
The real danger is the drink, not the food: alcohol shows up in up to seventy percent of adult water deaths.

description:
What if you swam right after eating? The waiting rule dates back at least to 1908's Scouting for Boys, but the American Red Cross Scientific Advisory Council found eating before swimming doesn't raise drowning risk.
Alcohol, on the other hand, is involved in up to 70% of water-recreation deaths among teens and adults (CDC).
What should we run through next?
first_comment: How long did your parents make you wait? Which childhood rule should we put through a what-if next?
